records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.text:
A-stability and L-stability describe the response of a time integrator to
linear decay modes. L1, L2 and L∞ instead describe the size and distribution
of an error. They answer different questions. A method can be stable with a
large error, and a small algebraic residual need not imply a small PDE error.
A/L-stability classification and accurate wave amplitudes and speeds are separate questions. For reading the magnitude and argument of an amplification factor, see von Neumann analysis: dissipation and dispersion basics.

records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.section: A-stability concerns the whole left half-plane#
records.text:
Apply a one-step method to y′=λy, with z=λΔt. Its stability function satisfies
y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n,\qquad
\mathcal S=\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\leq1\}.
The method is A-stable if its absolute-stability region contains the entire
closed left half-plane. In particular, R must have no pole there. Thus a
scalar mode with Re λ≤0 does not grow for any positive step size in this test.
Dahlquist (1963) is a foundational
A-stability reference in the linear-multistep setting. The one-step notation
here is used to make the comparison transparent.
Forward Euler, R(z)=1+z, is stable on the negative real axis only for
−2≤z≤0. No consistent explicit RK method is A-stable: its nonconstant
stability polynomial is unbounded along the negative real axis.
Being implicit alone does not guarantee A-stability.

records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.section: L-stability also damps infinitely stiff modes#
records.text:
An L-stable one-step method is A-stable and satisfies
\lim_{|z|\to\infty,\;\operatorname{Re}z<0}R(z)=0.
This extra property damps modes that are much faster than the chosen step.
Backward Euler has R(z)=1/(1−z), so it is both A-stable and L-stable.
Crank–Nicolson / the trapezoidal rule has
R_{CN}(z)=\frac{1+z/2}{1-z/2},\qquad
\lim_{z\to-\infty}R_{CN}(z)=-1.
It is A-stable but not L-stable: very stiff negative-real modes alternate
sign and decay only slowly. Implicit midpoint has the same scalar linear
R(z), although its nonlinear update is different from the trapezoidal rule.
For z=−1000, backward Euler gives about 0.001 in one step, while CN gives
about −0.996; the exact factor is exp(−1000).
For the implemented SDIRK2,
\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2,\qquad
R(z)=\frac{1+(1-2\gamma)z}{(1-\gamma z)^2}.
Its poles are in the right half-plane, it is A-stable and its large-z limit
is zero. This is the L-stable two-stage family associated with
Alexander (1977).
BDF2 is a two-step method: analyze its characteristic roots and parasitic
mode, rather than assigning it an arbitrary single-valued R(z).
These are linear absolute-stability statements. Accuracy, nonlinear
contractivity, SSP/TVD inheritance, positivity and boundary stability require
their own checks. Eigenvalues alone can also miss transient growth of
nonnormal operators. An A-stable time step cannot repair an inconsistent

records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.section: Continuous L1, L2 and L∞ errors#
records.text:
For scalar error e(x)=u_h(x)−u_ref(x) on a domain Ω,
\|e\|_{L^1}=\int_\Omega |e|\,dV,\qquad
\|e\|_{L^2}=\left(\int_\Omega |e|^2\,dV\right)^{1/2},\qquad
\|e\|_{L^\infty}=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in\Omega}|e(x)|.
L1 measures integrated absolute error. L2 emphasizes larger deviations more
strongly. L∞ measures the worst error apart from measure-zero sets. For a
continuous error on a compact domain, the essential supremum equals the maximum.
For discontinuous solutions, the value assigned exactly at a jump does not
change the continuous norm.
For a domain with volume V, mean absolute error is L1/V and RMS error is
L2/√V. These normalized quantities have the same physical units as u;
unnormalized integral norms also contain powers of length. State the convention
before comparing domains of different size.

records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.section: Discrete weights and the reference representation#
records.text:
For finite-volume error e_i between a numerical cell mean and a reference cell
mean, with positive cell volumes V_i,
E_1=\sum_iV_i|e_i|,\qquad
E_2=\left(\sum_iV_i|e_i|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad
E_\infty=\max_i|e_i|.
On a uniform grid, V_i=h^d. On the unit interval, these become mean absolute
error, RMS error and maximum cell-mean error. On a nonuniform mesh, an unweighted
arithmetic mean generally gives the wrong spatial weighting. For e=(1,3) and
cell volumes (0.75,0.25), E1=1.5, E2=√3 and E∞=3; unweighted means disagree.
The Euclidean vector norm np.linalg.norm(e) omits the h^(d/2) factor of a
physical discrete L2 norm. Comparing that raw norm across meshes can therefore
change an apparent convergence exponent. Relative error E_p/||u_ref||_p needs
a stated reference norm; when the denominator is zero, it is undefined. Any
regularization must be explicitly reported.
A reference at cell centers is not an exact cell-average reference. DG and FEM
need reconstruction and quadrature inside elements; a coefficient-vector
norm is not automatically a function L2 norm. Likewise, a maximum over sample
points is a sampled L∞ diagnostic, not necessarily the exact supremum of a
high-order reconstructed field. Vector components with different units should
be reported separately or nondimensionalized with stated scales.

records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.text:
For matched runs at the same physical time and error convention, the observed
order is
p_{obs}=\frac{\log(E_{coarse}/E_{fine})}{\log(h_{coarse}/h_{fine})}.
Temporal error, reference error, quadrature error, roundoff and incomplete
iterative convergence can mask spatial order. Refine time separately, or state
how Δt scales with h. Adaptive ODE tolerance is a local, component-scaled error
control; it is not a global spatial L2 error bound.
Different norms can behave differently near shocks. For example, an O(1)
error supported on width O(h) has L1=O(h), L2=O(√h) and L∞=O(1). This simple
scaling is not a universal convergence-rate claim for a shock solver. A useful
L1 refinement result need not imply maximum-norm convergence of a shifted jump.
For Ax=b, the residual is r=b−Ax. The solution error satisfies
x_num−x_exact=−A^(−1)r, so conditioning matters. An algebraic residual compares
against the discrete equation; discretization error compares that equation's
solution against the continuous problem. See sparse/nonlinear solvers
and the Lax–Richtmyer discussion.

records.title: A-stability, L-stability and error norms
records.section: Where the atlas reports each quantity#
records.text:
The equation gallery reports L1/MAE, L2/RMS and
L∞ over its stored unit-interval profiles. Its labels retain the distinction
between exact cell means, point-sampled Euler references and absent references.
The browser stability laboratory has a point-sampled
L1/MAE diagnostic and amplification factors; it does not thereby measure
a reconstructed finite-volume function norm.
P1 FEM integrates L2 and H1 seminorm errors inside triangles.
Periodic MAC flow reports a combined velocity RMS error
and maximum absolute discrete divergence. These are different diagnostics.
Stiff integration reports maximum error over accepted
time nodes, separate from nonlinear stage residuals and local step estimates.
Original exhibits keep their documented conventions; this chapter does not
retroactively relabel point samples as cell averages or certify a missing
maximum-norm calculation.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.text: Compute how a converged numerical solution responds to a changing coefficient. Implement implicit state sensitivities and a discrete adjoint gradient for Bratu’s equation, then check them against an exact continuous family, re-solved parameter differences and spatial refinement.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.text:
Consider a state u defined by an equation depending on parameters θ rather than by an explicit formula. For n states and m parameters, denote residual partial derivatives by J and B. All gradients below are column vectors.
F(u(\theta),\theta)=0,\qquad J=F_u\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},\qquad B=F_\theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}.
If F is continuously differentiable near the solution and J is nonsingular, the implicit function theorem defines a local derivative of the solution. Applying the chain rule gives a sensitivity equation. This does not establish global uniqueness or automatically select one branch among several roots.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Implicit differentiation: solve the sensitivity equation
records.text:
J S+B=0,\qquad S=\frac{du}{d\theta},\qquad J s_v=-Bv,\qquad s_v=S v.
S is the state Jacobian with respect to all parameters. If only one direction v is needed, solve one linear system with right-hand side −Bv. Do not explicitly form an inverse of J. Analytic expressions, AD or appropriately checked finite differences can supply J and B.
The example first solves the primal problem using the existing Newton method, then assembles residual partial derivatives at the computed state. AD evaluates local derivatives of the residual. The implementation does not differentiate an unrolled finite sequence of Newton iterations.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Discrete adjoints: obtain an objective gradient
records.text:
Observation fitting and design often need the total derivative of a scalar objective rather than every state sensitivity. Separate the partial derivative r at fixed state from the contribution Sᵀq due to the changing state.
\widehat L(\theta)=L(u(\theta),\theta),\qquad q=\nabla_uL,\quad r=\nabla_\theta L,\qquad \nabla_\theta\widehat L=r+S^Tq.
Solving a transpose system gives the same gradient without storing every column of S. The Lagrangian convention used here subtracts the residual term, so the term involving B has a minus sign.
J^Tp=q,\qquad \boxed{\nabla_\theta\widehat L=r-B^Tp}.
\mathcal L(u,\theta,p)=L(u,\theta)-p^TF(u,\theta),\qquad \nabla_u\mathcal L=q-J^Tp=0.
With many parameters and few objectives, adjoint solves per objective can replace sensitivity solves per parameter. Factorizations can be shared across right-hand sides, and a VJP can evaluate Bᵀp. This one-parameter, one-objective example has one right-hand side for either method and makes no speed claim. The implementation assembles and solves small dense matrices.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: The same Bratu discretization and branch
records.text:
Use the same Bratu equation on [0,1] with zero Dirichlet data as in the AD chapter. Here n counts interior unknowns. Coordinates, state, parameter and objective are dimensionless in this educational model. The grid and boundary data are independent of the parameter.
-u^{\prime\prime}-\lambda e^u=0,\quad 0<x<1,\quad u(0)=u(1)=0,\qquad F_i=\frac{2u_i-u_{i-1}-u_{i+1}}{h^2}-\lambda e^{u_i},\quad h=\frac1{n+1}.
J=D-\lambda\operatorname{diag}(e^u),\qquad D=h^{-2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1),\qquad F_\lambda=-e^u,\qquad J s=e^u.
The continuous problem has an exact family parameterized by α. The point α=1 uses the same parameter as the earlier Bratu example. The verification uses α=1 and 2, both corresponding to the smaller-solution branch reached from zero initial data.
u_\alpha(x)=-2\log\!\frac{\cosh(\alpha(x-1/2))}{\cosh(\alpha/2)},\qquad \lambda(\alpha)=\frac{2\alpha^2}{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)},
\frac{d\lambda}{d\alpha}=\lambda\left(\frac2\alpha-\tanh\frac\alpha2\right),\qquad s_*(x)=\frac{\tanh(\alpha/2)-2(x-1/2)\tanh(\alpha(x-1/2))}{d\lambda/d\alpha}.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: The same Bratu discretization and branch
records.text: Evaluate s_* at the grid nodes as an independent reference for the discrete sensitivity s. The continuous solution is not assumed to be an exact root of the discrete equations. Sensitivity can diverge at a fold where dλ/dα vanishes. Branch switching, passage through singular points and continuation of the upper branch are outside the verified scope.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Retain the objective’s explicit parameter dependence
records.text:
L_h(u,\lambda)=\frac h2\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i^2+\frac\beta2\lambda^2,\qquad \beta=0.05,\qquad q=h u,\quad r=\beta\lambda.
The first term is a trapezoidal approximation of the integral of half the squared state. Zero endpoint values leave only interior contributions. The second term deliberately retains explicit parameter dependence, so dropping βλ can be detected separately from the state-mediated contribution. This is a defined derivative-check objective, not a fit to observational data.
J^Tp=h u,\qquad g_{\mathrm{direct}}=\beta\lambda+h u^T s,\qquad g_{\mathrm{adjoint}}=\beta\lambda+p^T e^u.
Here p is a discrete adjoint in the Euclidean inner product; the quadrature weight h is included in q=h u. Do not identify p directly with nodal values of a continuous PDE adjoint defined in an L² inner product. Nonuniform grids, finite elements and parameter-dependent quadrature require consistent treatment of mass matrices and weights.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Verification: separate sensitivities, gradients and spatial error
records.text:
The saved measurements and source hashes record controls, tested points, residuals and errors.
Residual partial derivatives. Treat state and parameter as independent inputs; compare AD evaluations of J and F_λ with analytic expressions. A parameter-only seed holds u fixed.
Sensitivity and adjoint equations. Use the same converged state and recompute each linear-system residual. Compare direct and adjoint gradients, including the explicit βλ term.
Parameter differences. Solve the nonlinear problem again at λ+ε and λ−ε before differencing the objective. Perturbing λ while holding the state fixed does not test the total derivative.
Spatial refinement. For n=15, 31 and 63 compare discrete sensitivity with the exact continuous s_* in the maximum nodal norm. Direct–adjoint agreement alone does not establish spatial accuracy.
Saved measurements. The points α=1 and 2 have λ≈1.5728955 and 3.3597947. All six regular cases start at zero with an absolute primal residual Euclidean tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰ and at most 40 updates. Direct and adjoint gradients differ by less than 1.4×10⁻¹⁵. Primal residuals are at most 5.3×10⁻¹¹; the relative sensitivity and adjoint residuals defined below are at most 2.3×10⁻¹³ and 1.9×10⁻¹³, respectively.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Verification: separate sensitivities, gradients and spatial error
records.text:
For n=15, 31 and 63, maximum nodal sensitivity errors are approximately 3.0015×10⁻⁴, 7.4860×10⁻⁵ and 1.8704×10⁻⁵ at α=1; at α=2 they are 2.6708×10⁻², 6.4898×10⁻³ and 1.6112×10⁻³. Halving h reduces errors by about four; the coarser α=2 grid shows a larger departure from the asymptotic regime. These are spatial sensitivity errors, not direct–adjoint discrepancies.
g_{\mathrm{FD}}(\varepsilon)=\frac{L_h(u(\lambda+\varepsilon),\lambda+\varepsilon)-L_h(u(\lambda-\varepsilon),\lambda-\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}.
The n=31 difference check uses 17 perturbations ε from 10⁻¹ to 10⁻⁹. In this saved run, agreement is good near ε=10⁻⁵, where the absolute gradient difference for α=2 is about 4.0×10⁻¹¹. At ε=10⁻⁹ it grows to about 1.3×10⁻⁶. Making perturbations ever smaller does not give an ever more accurate gradient.
The parameter perturbation ε and spatial mesh spacing h are different quantities. Sweep ε and vary the nonlinear solve tolerance to expose regimes dominated by truncation, incomplete convergence or roundoff. Finite differences provide an independent check, not a uniformly optimal reference at every perturbation.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Verification: separate sensitivities, gradients and spatial error
records.text:
The Bratu Jacobian here is symmetric, so replacing Jᵀ incorrectly by J would escape detection on this problem alone. A separate manufactured implicit system with a nonsymmetric matrix and multiple parameters therefore independently checks direct sensitivities and adjoint gradients. That test checks transposition, signs and shapes; it does not validate another physical model.
A separate α=2, n=31 sweep uses primal tolerances 10⁻², 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻¹⁰. At ε=10⁻⁴, absolute finite-difference gradient error decreases from about 3.2×10⁻⁵ for the loose 10⁻² solve to about 3.5×10⁻⁸ for the two tighter settings. The 10⁻⁶ and 10⁻¹⁰ controls accept the same Newton iterates, so their curves overlap. Do not interpret every tolerance tightening as a distinct result or a strict monotonic improvement.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.section: Incomplete solves, conditioning and unrolled iterations
records.text:
r_F=\|F(u,\lambda)\|_2,\qquad \rho_s=\frac{\|Js+F_\lambda\|_2}{\|F_\lambda\|_2},\qquad \rho_p=\frac{\|J^Tp-q\|_2}{\|q\|_2}.
Primal, sensitivity and adjoint equations have separate residuals. A small linear residual does not repair an unconverged state: derivatives are then evaluated at an approximate state rather than an exact root. An ill-conditioned J can amplify small primal errors into state or gradient errors. Conditioning also depends on scaling and grid size, so cross-grid condition numbers are not algorithm rankings.
Differentiating finitely many iterations gives the derivative of a map depending on the initial state and executed updates. Implicit differentiation targets the equations defining a local converged solution. State that distinction when differentiating through stopping criteria, line searches or adaptive decisions. A computed gradient alone establishes neither inverse-problem identifiability nor optimizer convergence.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.text:
-s^{\prime\prime}-\lambda e^u s=e^u,\qquad s(0)=s(1)=0.
Differentiating the continuous Bratu equation with respect to λ gives this boundary-value problem. Here centered differences also provide its natural discretization, and refinement can be checked against s_* from the exact family. In general, discretizing a continuous adjoint and differentiating a discrete residual need not agree on a finite mesh. Include parameter dependence of boundaries, grids, observation operators and quadrature weights.
Verified scope is a specified smooth steady Bratu branch and a small nonsymmetric manufactured system. It does not cover shocks, limiters, contacts/events, transient adjoints, singular bifurcation points or inverse fitting to real observations. Read discretization error, derivative implementation and physical-model validity separately.
A separate continuous reference is also provided for the objective gradient. Integrate the exact-family u_α and s_* and compare 96- and 192-point Gauss quadrature.
g_* =\beta\lambda+\int_0^1 u_\alpha(x)s_*(x)\,dx.

records.title: Implicit differentiation and adjoints: Bratu parameter sensitivity
records.text: The references are about 0.1027083914 at α=1 and 0.5823748758 at α=2. The n=31 discrete adjoint gradients are about 0.1027218294 and 0.5857608186, respectively. Spatial error remains despite near-machine-precision direct–adjoint agreement. The two quadrature orders differ by less than 4.4×10⁻¹⁵ in both cases; their difference is a convergence diagnostic rather than a rigorous quadrature error bound.

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.section: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.text:
The limiter notebook
includes a TVB scalar experiment and a separate conservative Euler-state
scaling demonstration. These address different failure modes: loss of accuracy
near a smooth extremum and inadmissible thermodynamic states.

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.text:
For a candidate increment v and neighboring increments a and b, define
\widetilde m(v,a,b)=
\begin{cases}
v,&|v|\le M\Delta x^2,\\
m(v,a,b),&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
where m is the generalized minmod: the smallest magnitude with a shared sign,
and zero when signs disagree. Our scalar demonstration chooses v=(a+b)/2.
At M=0 this reduces to the two-increment minmod used in the TVD experiment.
At M>0 sufficiently small increments survive even when the neighboring slopes
have opposite signs, permitting a smooth peak to remain curved.
The dx-squared threshold reflects the scale of smooth-extremum face
deviations in the RKDG setting. Its coefficient has units of solution divided
by length squared; it is not a universal dimensionless constant. Rescaling the
dependent variable or coordinates requires reconsidering M. Increments and
derivatives require different thresholds.
Cockburn and Shu (1989)
develop the TVB RKDG framework. This edition implements the modified-minmod
building block in scalar finite volumes, rather than that full RKDG method
or its theorem. The notebook computes M=0,10,50 on both the sine and square
pulse. Compare errors and measured maximum TV: allowing small extrema means
TV need not decrease at every step, and a large M can also admit small
oscillations beside a discontinuity. Changing M does not prove a uniform TVB

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.text: bound for an arbitrary method. No Euler-system TVB extension is implemented.

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.section: Positive density and pressure are different constraints#
records.text:
For ideal-gas conservative variables U=(rho,m,E),
p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{|m|^2}{2\rho}\right),\qquad
\mathcal G=\{U:\rho>0,\ p(U)>0\}.
Positive density alone does not ensure positive internal energy. TVD, TVB,
an entropy fix, and the absence of visible wiggles do not automatically make
Euler states admissible. A negative pressure can arise from excessive kinetic
energy even when rho and E are positive.

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.text:
Start with an admissible conservative cell average Ubar. Scale every supplied
reconstruction point by the same factor:
\widehat U_\alpha=\bar U+\theta(U_\alpha-\bar U),\qquad 0\le\theta\le1.
If the original points have quadrature mean Ubar, the scaled points retain it.
Using a single theta across components and points is essential to this
particular construction. Clipping rho, pressure, or total energy independently
does not have that conservation property.
First bound theta by the minimum reconstructed density:
\theta_\rho=\min\left(1,
\frac{\bar\rho-\epsilon_\rho}{\bar\rho-\rho_{\min}}\right)
\quad\text{if }\rho_{\min}<\epsilon_\rho;
\qquad\theta_\rho=1\text{ otherwise}.
Then shrink theta in [0,theta_rho] until every supplied point also satisfies
p(Uhat) ≥ epsilon_p. Ideal-gas pressure is concave for positive density, so
the admissible part of this line segment contains the mean and can be found
by bisection. The implementation uses 64 iterations and a small roundoff
retreat. Density and pressure floors are input parameters, not inserted mass
or energy. Inadmissible averages raise an error; scaling around a bad mean
cannot repair conservation and positivity together in this way.
This follows the convex-scaling idea of
Zhang and Shu (2010), with a
deliberately simple common-state scaling and numerical pressure search. It is

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.text:
not a line-by-line reproduction of their two-stage density-polynomial and
state limiter. The implementation covers the supplied points only; arbitrary
polynomial values between those points are not automatically bounded.

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.text:
The three-node cell has xi=-1,0,1, positive Gauss–Lobatto weights
(1/6,2/3,1/6), gamma=1.4, and Ubar=(1,0,2.5). The raw states are
Ubar + xi times delta. Choose delta=(1.2,0,0) for a density violation,
(0,3,0) for a pressure violation, or (1.2,3,1) for a combined violation.
Their weighted mean is exactly Ubar in real arithmetic. The plot samples only
these three nodes and reports theta, minimum limited density, minimum limited
pressure, and the conservative mean defect, with epsilon_rho=epsilon_p=1e-8.
These are constructed reconstruction tests, not blast-wave or rarefaction
time integrations.
import numpy as np
from numart.limiters import positive_reconstruction
mean = np.array([1., 0., 2.5])
raw = mean + np.array([-1., 0., 1.])[:, None] * [0., 3., 0.]
limited, theta = positive_reconstruction(mean, raw)
Tests check that an already admissible reconstruction is unchanged, bad means
are rejected, and both floors and conservative quadrature means survive the
three failure cases.

records.title: Advanced limiters: TVB and positivity preservation
records.section: From reconstruction to a fully discrete guarantee#
records.text:
A complete positivity-preserving Euler method also needs a compatible
positivity-preserving numerical flux, positive quadrature decomposition
including interface states, a corresponding wave-speed/CFL restriction, and
limiting at all required stages. SSP time stepping propagates a forward-Euler
positivity property only when that property and its step restriction already
hold. Source terms and boundary treatment require their own checks.
This helper is not wired into the existing Euler MUSCL, finite-difference
WENO, CT/GLM, or KEEP time updates. Those solvers retain their documented
limitations. A future complete implementation should add stage-by-stage
admissibility and conservation checks, near-vacuum double rarefaction, and
strong blast-wave tests before claiming positivity preservation over time.
Multidimensional and non-ideal-EOS extensions need additional analysis.

records.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
records.text:
For Ax=b, the 2-norm condition number is κ₂(A)=σmax/σmin. It measures
sensitivity to perturbations rather than the convergence rate of a particular
iteration. Left preconditioning gives P^{-1}Ax=P^{-1}b; right preconditioning
gives AP^{-1}y=b, x=P^{-1}y. For symmetric positive-definite systems,
P^{-1/2}AP^{-1/2} supports symmetry-preserving comparisons.
conditioning_example constructs A=S B S, where B is a 1D Poisson matrix
and S is diagonal scaling. It demonstrates the change in condition number
under symmetric Jacobi scaling. It does not implement Turkel's low-Mach flow
preconditioning matrix.
Compressible PDEs pose a separate preconditioning problem when low-Mach
convective and acoustic characteristic speeds differ greatly. A pseudo-time
system such as Γ(U) ∂U/∂τ + R(U)=0 modifies characteristic speeds,
convergence, and numerical dissipation. Deriving Γ, transforming variables,
choosing Mach-dependent coefficients, and maintaining boundary consistency
require additional verification. Replacing the physical time derivative
indiscriminately changes the time-dependent solution.
Turkel (1987).

records.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
records.text:
Applying BDF2 in physical time to dU/dt+R(U)=0 gives
\frac{3U^{n+1}-4U^n+U^{n-1}}{2\Delta t}+R(U^{n+1})=0.
At each physical step, evolve the pseudo-time equation for Q,
\frac{dQ}{d\tau}+\frac{3Q-4U^n+U^{n-1}}{2\Delta t}+R(Q)=0,
to a steady state. Backward Euler starts the first step. Physical-time accuracy
depends on Δt, spatial error, and incomplete inner convergence. A large physical
CFL alone does not establish accurate time evolution.
Jameson (1991).
dual_time_advection is a minimal periodic 1D example: implicit upwind
advection with BDF1/BDF2, solved by a Jacobi pseudo-time iteration. The inner
residual threshold is tol*max(1,||b||∞), with default tol=1e-10. Failure to
converge within the iteration limit raises an error. Tests compare against an
independent dense solve of the BDF2 discrete equations. This is a reduced model
rather than Jameson's complete compressible-flow multigrid algorithm.

records.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
records.text:
Distribute an element residual Φ_K=∫K ∇·F(U) dV to its nodes while preserving
Σ_{i∈K} Φ_i^K=Φ_K. This conservation condition connects continuous finite
elements with upwind ideas.
Abgrall (2006), author-hosted review.
rd_residual is a minimal 1D P1 scalar-advection example. It assigns all of
Φ_K=a(u_{i+1}-u_i) to the downstream node and divides by lumped mass h.
Tests establish equivalence to first-order upwind differences in this case.
2D triangular N/LDA schemes, nonlinear blending, time-consistent mass matrices,
and Euler systems remain unimplemented.

records.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
records.section: Roe, entropy fixes, Einfeldt, and rotated solvers#
records.text:
Roe uses a linearization satisfying F_R-F_L=Ã(U_R-U_L) and its eigensystem.
This edition forms sqrt(ρ)-weighted u and H, with
ã²=(γ-1)(H̃-ũ²/2), and adds dissipation through wave strengths and
eigenvectors.
Roe (1981).
The entropy fix replaces the absolute acoustic eigenvalue below δ with
(λ²+δ²)/(2δ). HLLE is a separate flux using Einfeldt-type left/right wave
speeds for strong low-density expansions. Roe entropy correction, HLLE
positivity properties, and carbuncle treatments address different problems.
Einfeldt (1988),
Einfeldt et al. (1991).
Rotated-hybrid Riemann solvers combine fluxes using directions beyond the face
normal to balance shock robustness and shear-layer resolution. A coordinate
rotation alone does not reproduce this construction. This edition adds a specified directional HLLE/Roe composition and cylinder-forebody tests. This explicit two-flux experiment is distinct from an optimized reproduction of the original Rotated-RHLL dissipation formula.
Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008).

records.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
records.text:
Roe's 1981 paper, author-uploaded full text, pp. 359–360
uses four conditions: (i) a linear mapping from conserved-state space to
flux space for each fixed state pair; (ii) the coincident-state limit equals
the physical Jacobian; (iii) the matrix maps the state jump exactly onto
the flux jump; (iv) its eigenvectors are linearly independent. The two-state
matrix need not depend linearly on its arguments. For physical ideal-gas Euler
states the construction below also has real acoustic/contact speeds.
Here is the algebra implemented and independently checked in this atlas.
For U=(ρ,ρu,E), H=(E+p)/ρ, set z=√ρ(1,u,H). Then
 U(z)=\begin{pmatrix}z_1^2\\z_1z_2\\
 (z_1z_3+(\gamma-1)z_2^2/2)/\gamma\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 F(z)=\begin{pmatrix}z_1z_2\\
 ((\gamma+1)z_2^2/2+(\gamma-1)z_1z_3)/\gamma\\z_2z_3\end{pmatrix}.
Both maps are quadratic. Their midpoint Jacobians B=∂U/∂z and C=∂F/∂z
therefore satisfy ΔU=B(z̄)Δz and ΔF=C(z̄)Δz exactly. Consequently
Ã=C(z̄)B(z̄)⁻¹ has the jump property. Ratios of z̄ give
 \widetilde u=\frac{\sqrt{\rho_L}u_L+\sqrt{\rho_R}u_R}{\sqrt{\rho_L}+\sqrt{\rho_R}},\quad
 \widetilde H=\frac{\sqrt{\rho_L}H_L+\sqrt{\rho_R}H_R}{\sqrt{\rho_L}+\sqrt{\rho_R}},\quad
 \widetilde c^2=(\gamma-1)(\widetilde H-\widetilde u^2/2).
At equal states, the chain rule gives CB⁻¹=∂F/∂U. The independently constructed

records.title: Preconditioning, dual time stepping, and residual distribution
records.text:
eigenbasis has speeds ũ−c̃,ũ,ũ+c̃. Since c̃>0, its three eigenvectors span
the state space. We check the parameter-vector matrix against this eigenbasis,
the analytic Jacobian, and 2000 deterministic physical state pairs.
If ΔF=sΔU for a single nonzero Rankine–Hugoniot jump, then ÃΔU=sΔU:
the jump lies in the speed-s eigenspace. The unmodified Roe flux consequently
recognizes isolated contact/shock jumps. This does not make every reconstructed,
time-discretized shock calculation exact. Smoothing |λ| changes the flux
without changing the matrix identity, and can smear a stationary shock.
An expansion discontinuity can also satisfy the jump relation. Our reversed
stationary normal-shock pair passes Property U but the raw Roe flux differs
from the entropy Riemann reference. This is a numerical counterexample to
confusing the jump property with entropy selection. The entropy fix is an
additional design choice; neither gives a multidimensional carbuncle guarantee.
python scripts/build_shock_robustness.py saves the matrix checks, moving and
stationary shocks, a contact and the expansion counterexample in the
diagnostic manifest.
Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment

records.title: Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods
records.text: Eulerian cells stay fixed while fluid crosses their faces. Lagrangian cells move with the fluid. In ALE, the mesh velocity w can be chosen independently of the fluid velocity u. Hirt, Amsden, and Cook (1974) provide a classical all-speed ALE formulation.

records.title: Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods
records.section: The flux is relative to the moving face#
records.text:
Reynolds transport gives, for a moving control volume K(t),
\frac{d}{dt}\int_{K(t)}U\,dV
+\int_{\partial K(t)}\left[F(U)\cdot n-(w\cdot n)U\right]dS=0.
With w = 0 this is Eulerian. Choosing the normal mesh speed equal to the fluid normal speed gives the Lagrangian mass-flux limit. Pressure still transfers momentum and energy across a material face; setting mass flux to zero does not set every Euler flux to zero.

records.title: Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods
records.section: Geometry must obey a conservation law too#
records.text:
For a uniform state to remain uniform, changing cell volumes and face motion must agree:
\frac{d|K|}{dt}=\int_{\partial K}w\cdot n\,dS.
Its discrete counterpart is the geometric conservation law (GCL). A mesh-motion routine and a flow update that use inconsistent swept volumes can create a spurious flow from constant data, even if each looks accurate separately.

records.title: Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods
records.text:
numart.geometry.moving_volume_uniform_test deforms faces on [0,1] by a smooth sinusoidal displacement with fixed endpoints. Face velocity is the actual displacement divided by delta t. For constant scalar q, it updates the extensive quantity Vq with relative flux (a−w)q and divides by the new volume. The same displacement appears in both operations.
import numpy as np
from numart.geometry import moving_volume_uniform_test
old_faces, new_faces, q = moving_volume_uniform_test(phase=0.8)
print(np.max(np.abs(q - 1)))
Uniform-state preservation is checked to roundoff over several deformation phases. The amplitude restriction ensures positive cell widths. This is a 1D moving-volume identity check, not an ALE Euler solver or a test of accuracy for nonuniform data.

records.title: Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian methods
records.text:
A complete ALE method may move vertices, solve a Lagrangian or relative-flux step, and remap to a better mesh. Conservative remapping, mesh tangling, boundary motion, and temporal consistency require additional tests. A remap that preserves total mass can still violate positivity or fail to preserve a constant state.
Use the mesh chapter to separate topology from motion, and the coordinate chapter to distinguish moving control volumes from changing tensor bases. Neither replacing x by r nor moving plotted vertices automatically constructs an ALE method.

records.title: Algebraic multigrid / AMG
records.text: AMG constructs a multilevel hierarchy and interpolation from a matrix. Smooth error means error that relaxation removes poorly, rather than only geometrically long-wavelength error.

records.title: Algebraic multigrid / AMG
records.text:
For Au=b, use residual r=b−Au, restriction R and interpolation P. The Galerkin coarse operator is A_c=RAP. Correct the fine approximation using a coarse residual solve. The inverse in the formula expresses the principle; a multilevel cycle normally approximates that solve recursively.
A_c=RAP,\qquad r=b-Au,\qquad u\leftarrow u+P A_c^{-1}Rr.

records.title: Algebraic multigrid / AMG
records.text: A cycle applies pre-relaxation, computes/restricts the residual, corrects on the coarse space and post-relaxes. Classical AMG uses strength connections and C/F splitting; aggregation variants group unknowns. Near-nullspace information, such as rigid motions for elasticity, must be represented by interpolation.

records.title: Algebraic multigrid / AMG
records.text:
Success on a scalar elliptic problem does not ensure robustness for nonsymmetric advection, saddle points or strong anisotropy. CG preconditioning requires compatible symmetry/positive-definiteness properties. A pure-Neumann problem still has a constant nullspace and a right-hand-side compatibility condition.
Condition number alone does not determine AMG performance. Anisotropy direction, strength selection, the near-nullspace represented by interpolation and relaxation all affect convergence, even for positive-definite systems. Fixed isotropic/anisotropic matrix controls do not certify arbitrary elliptic problems or large parallel calculations.

records.title: Algebraic multigrid / AMG
records.text:
Use manufactured Poisson solutions while varying mesh size and coefficient contrast. Measure true residuals, solution errors and per-cycle reduction; record hierarchy sizes and nonzero counts. Few iterations do not establish small discretization error.
Preserve the historical manufactured-Poisson example. The additional release forms right-hand sides from known algebraic solutions and compares linear solves with an independent sparse direct solver and discrete-sine-transform diagonalization, also checking the analytic discrete spectrum. Record true relative residual, relative solution error, iteration history and hierarchy complexity separately while varying matrix size, anisotropy and conditioning at fixed residual tolerance and iteration budget. This added case is an algebraic conditioning diagnostic; it does not establish mesh convergence or accuracy against the continuous Poisson solution.

records.text:
Computation for a fixed target
Build a smoothed-aggregation hierarchy from an SPD matrix alone and run V-cycles. Problems with 7², 15² and 31² unknowns distinguish independent sparse direct solutions, analytic discrete sine modes and second-order convergence to the continuum solution.
Only three fixed scalar grids are checked. Large coefficient jumps, strong anisotropy, elasticity, arbitrary unstructured meshes, optimal complexity and mesh-independent convergence are not certified. A small residual alone does not prove a small solution error.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.text:
Automatic differentiation (AD) evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule
to the elementary operations in a program. It supplies Jacobians for Newton
iterations, directional derivatives for Krylov methods, and sensitivities for
parameter estimation. These are shared numerical foundations across many
physical models.
Implemented here: a small forward-mode dual-number engine and a comparison
of analytic differentiation, finite differences and AD on the existing Bratu
boundary-value problem. The experiment reuses the atlas's Armijo-damped Newton
solver. Reverse mode, implicit sensitivities and adjoints are explained as
connections; this exhibit does not implement them.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Four ways to obtain a derivative
records.text:
An analytic derivative is derived mathematically and entered into the
solver by hand. It can expose structure and provide an independent reference,
but the derivative must be kept consistent with the residual implementation.
Symbolic differentiation manipulates expressions into another expression.
AD instead carries numerical derivative information through the evaluated
operations, without constructing a global symbolic formula.
Finite differences estimate a derivative from perturbed function values.
For a vector residual F and a direction v, forward and centered differences are
D_\varepsilon^+F(u)v=\frac{F(u+\varepsilon v)-F(u)}{\varepsilon},
\qquad
D_\varepsilon^0F(u)v=\frac{F(u+\varepsilon v)-F(u-\varepsilon v)}{2\varepsilon}.
For sufficiently smooth F, their truncation errors are first and second order
in ε. A very small ε amplifies cancellation and rounding in the residual
evaluations. The useful step depends on the state, direction, precision and
scaling of F. A finite-difference check should therefore sweep several steps.
AD has no finite-difference step or associated truncation error. It still uses
floating-point arithmetic: unstable formulas, overflow, underflow and rounding
can affect both values and derivatives. The differentiated object is the
composition of real-arithmetic operations represented by the executed program,

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Four ways to obtain a derivative
records.text:
evaluated numerically. It is not the derivative of the discontinuous mapping
from one set of floating-point bit patterns to another.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Forward mode: carry a value and a direction
records.text:
Seed the input with a direction v and propagate pairs consisting of a value
and its directional derivative. Dual-number notation makes the chain rule
visible:
\widehat a=a+\eta\dot a,\qquad \eta^2=0,
\qquad
\widehat a\widehat b=ab+\eta(\dot a b+a\dot b),
\qquad
\exp(\widehat a)=\exp(a)+\eta\exp(a)\dot a.
The nilpotent symbol η is an algebraic device, not a small numerical step.
The implementation stores the two arrays separately. It overloads the small
set of operations needed for this experiment, including elementwise
arithmetic, indexing, exponentiation and multiplication by a constant matrix.
Unsupported operations are outside this educational engine's scope.
For F from n inputs to m outputs, one seeded execution returns F(u) and J(u)v.
This Jacobian–vector product (JVP) avoids storing an m-by-n Jacobian. Seed
each coordinate basis vector in turn to assemble all n columns. The Bratu
comparison deliberately uses that transparent assembly; it does not exploit
sparsity coloring or provide a matrix-free Newton solver.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Reverse mode and the derivative you actually need
records.text:
Reverse mode propagates an output weight w backwards through local derivative
rules to obtain J(u)ᵀw, often called a vector–Jacobian product (VJP). For
a scalar objective with many parameters, one reverse pass can produce its
gradient. An implementation commonly retains intermediate values or
recomputes them through checkpointing. Forward mode is attractive when only
a few input directions are required. The relevant dimensions are the numbers
of independent inputs and outputs, together with the requested products.
A Hessian–vector product for a smooth scalar objective can be obtained by
differentiating its gradient in a direction. Explicitly assembling a Hessian
is unnecessary when an optimization method only needs that product. See
Baydin et al. (2018) for an AD
survey and the JAX autodiff cookbook
for practical JVP, VJP and higher-order constructions. JAX is a reading
reference; the local experiment requires only the atlas's existing NumPy
environment.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.text:
We retain the same sign convention, parameter and exact solution used in the
sparse and nonlinear systems verification:
-u''(x)-\lambda e^{u(x)}=0,\qquad 0<x<1,\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0,
\qquad \lambda=\frac{2}{\cosh^2(1/2)},u_*(x)=-2\log\!\left(\frac{\cosh(x-1/2)}{\cosh(1/2)}\right).
Here n denotes the number of interior unknowns. The interval has n+1
uniform cells, with h=1/(n+1) and nodes x_i=ih. Centered differences give
F_i(u)=\frac{2u_i-u_{i-1}-u_{i+1}}{h^2}-\lambda e^{u_i},
\qquad u_0=u_{n+1}=0,J(u)=D-\lambda\operatorname{diag}(e^u),
\qquad D=\frac{1}{h^2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1).
The analytic Jacobian is an independent formula. Finite differences and AD
both evaluate the same residual function. In particular, AD differentiates
the discrete residual F; it does not remove the centered stencil's spatial
discretization error. The exact continuous solution is used to check spatial
refinement, not as an exact root of the discrete equations.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.text:
The saved measurements and source hashes separate
three checks so that accurate derivatives and accurate PDE solutions are not
confused.
The derivative check uses n=31 and the state u_*(x_i)+0.05 sin(3πx_i), away
from the exact continuous profile. Its direction is sin(2πx_i)+0.3 cos(5πx_i),
normalized to unit Euclidean length. The sweep contains 29 logarithmically
spaced, absolute perturbations from 1 down to 10⁻¹⁴; these are derivative
perturbations, not spatial mesh widths.
Differentiate at a fixed state. Compare the assembled forward-mode AD
Jacobian and its JVP against the analytic formula. Sweep finite-difference
steps at that same state, using both forward and centered differences.
Report relative Frobenius errors for matrices and relative Euclidean
errors for directional products. A deterministic smooth direction prevents
run-to-run changes in the comparison.
Solve the same discrete system. Start every Newton solve at zero, use
the same residual, Armijo search, dense linear solve and residual tolerance,
and change only how the Jacobian is supplied. The finite-difference run
uses a fixed centered-difference step recorded in the manifest. Measure
the true residual after each accepted iteration and compare the final
roots with the analytic-Jacobian solve.
Refine the mesh. Repeat the three methods for n=15, 31 and 63 interior

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.text:
nodes. Compare their roots with u_* at the interior nodes using a nodal
maximum error. Approximately fourfold error reduction under halving h
identifies the centered scheme's second-order spatial behavior.
In the saved run, AD and the analytic Jacobian agree entry by entry, while
the relative JVP error is about 8×10⁻¹⁶. This exact matrix agreement is
specific to the operation ordering in this example, not a general guarantee
of bitwise agreement for AD. The finite-difference curves show the useful
range between truncation error and cancellation. All nine Newton solves
reach the common absolute residual Euclidean tolerance 10⁻¹⁰ in three
updates. The fixed centered-difference perturbation is 10⁻⁵; its final roots
agree with the analytic-Jacobian roots to less than 10⁻¹⁴ in nodal maximum
norm. The continuous nodal maximum errors are approximately 1.738×10⁻⁴,
4.337×10⁻⁵ and 1.084×10⁻⁵ on the three grids. Their factor-of-four reduction
remains after changing the derivative calculation: spatial discretization
sets the leading solution error here.
The matrix norm includes entries of size h⁻². A small relative matrix error
can therefore hide errors in smaller terms. The direct directional check is
reported separately, rather than relying only on a product of the assembled
finite-difference matrix.
The analytic derivative is a reference, not an assumption that every analytic

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.text:
implementation is correct. The tests also check derivative rules on separate
functions and nontrivial directions, and check Bratu refinement against the
continuous solution. Agreement between two Jacobians alone would not validate
the boundary conditions or the PDE discretization.
The figure makes no speed ranking. Assembling a dense AD Jacobian here needs
n forward seeds; centered differences need two residual evaluations per
column. Counts describe these implementations, not equal-cost operations or
the best sparse AD strategy. For a large Newton–Krylov method, supplying Jv
directly can be preferable to constructing every column, while a suitable
preconditioner remains necessary.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Connections to implicit integration and parameter estimation
records.text:
An implicit ODE stage has a residual involving the
state and time step. Its Newton matrix contains derivatives of the ODE
right-hand side, so the same AD construction can supply them. For parameter
estimation, derivatives of observations or an objective with respect to model
parameters connect a simulation to an optimization method. Derivative
availability does not itself choose a stable integrator, a well-conditioned
parameterization or a convergent optimization algorithm.
Suppose the converged discrete state satisfies F(u,θ)=0. At a differentiable
solution with nonsingular F_u, its parameter sensitivity satisfies
F_u\frac{du}{d\theta}=-F_\theta.
For a scalar objective L(u,θ), an adjoint solve gives
F_u^T p=L_u^T,\qquad
\frac{dL}{d\theta}=L_\theta-p^TF_\theta.
This differentiates the equation defining the solution. Differentiating a
fixed, finite sequence of Newton iterations instead gives the derivative of
that sequence, including its dependence on the initial guess. Stopping
criteria and line-search branches complicate that distinction. Near a
singular Jacobian, sensitivities can be large even when the primal residual
is small. Primal and derivative solve tolerances therefore need separate
checks. These sensitivity and adjoint equations are explanatory extensions;
the present Bratu exhibit compares Jacobians used in the primal solve.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.section: Limits: smoothness, branches and numerical stability
records.text:
AD applies the derivative rules of the operations that are executed. At a
branch boundary, an absolute-value corner or a limiter switch, the underlying
function may have no unique classical derivative; a library's chosen rule
does not establish one. Adaptive time-step decisions can change the executed
path under parameter perturbations. For shocks, a computed grid-value
derivative also needs interpretation in terms of shock motion and the
quantity being measured.
The discretized derivative should be checked for mesh and time-step
convergence when it is intended to approximate a continuous sensitivity.
Differentiating a discretized solver and discretizing continuous sensitivity
or adjoint equations require their own consistency analysis. Stable function
evaluation matters too: a formula that overflows in the primal calculation
is not repaired by applying the chain rule.

records.title: Automatic differentiation: derivatives for numerical solvers
records.text:
Extract the November 22, 2026 release ZIP into a new folder. Prepare a Python environment with NumPy, Matplotlib and pytest, and run from the extracted folder. See the README for the complete instructions.
python -m pip install numpy matplotlib pytest
python scripts/build_autodiff.py
python -m pytest tests/test_autodiff.py
Read the AD engine and Bratu residual, existing Newton solver, figure and evidence builder, and test source individually. An independent-extraction verification record and source inventory and hashes accompany the package.
The builder writes the figure and a JSON manifest containing grids, parameters, finite-difference steps, stopping controls, norms, solver histories, the numerical environment and source SHA-256 hashes. Evidence is generated from the numerical implementation independently of the website build. The dated supplement includes the forward-mode engine, Bratu comparison, tests and saved results introduced here. Reverse-mode and adjoint solvers remain outside this implementation. Continue with Newton and conditioning, stiff integration, or the error-norm guide.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.section: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.text: A mesh supplies cells, geometry and connectivity. A basis supplies the functions used to represent a field on those cells. The choice of basis is separate from cell shape and variable staggering. The basis notebook makes modes, nodes and their mass matrices visible. The existing DG advection example already uses Legendre modes internally; this chapter exposes the algebra behind it.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.text:
Map a physical interval of length h and center x_c to a reference interval:
x=x_c+J\xi,\qquad J=h/2,\qquad -1\leq\xi\leq1,
\qquad u_h(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}a_j\phi_j(\xi).
The p+1 coefficients are element degrees of freedom. In a continuous finite-element method, neighboring elements share selected boundary degrees of freedom. DG keeps independent element coefficients and couples traces through numerical fluxes. A local polynomial basis can serve either formulation.
For constant material coefficients and an affine map, the element mass and diffusion matrices are
M_{ij}=J\int_{-1}^{1}\phi_i\phi_j\,d\xi,
\qquad K_{ij}=J^{-1}\int_{-1}^{1}\phi_i'\phi_j'\,d\xi.
Curved maps introduce a variable Jacobian; variable density or coefficients also change these integrals. Reference-element orthogonality alone then does not make the physical matrix diagonal.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.text:
With unit weight on [-1,1], the Legendre family satisfies
P_0=1,\quad P_1=\xi,\quad P_2=(3\xi^2-1)/2,
\qquad (n+1)P_{n+1}=(2n+1)\xi P_n-nP_{n-1},
\int_{-1}^{1}P_iP_j\,d\xi=\frac{2}{2i+1}\delta_{ij},
\qquad \widehat P_i=\sqrt{\frac{2i+1}{2}}P_i.
The ordinary Legendre mass is diagonal, with unequal diagonal entries. The orthonormal reference mass is the identity. Their coefficient values differ, although both span exactly the same degree-p polynomial space. The constant mode encodes the element mean; the higher Legendre modes have zero mean. See NIST DLMF §18.3 for normalization and §18.9 for recurrence relations.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.section: Nodal Lagrange functions represent the same space#
records.text:
Choose distinct nodes and define cardinal polynomials:
\ell_j(\xi)=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{\xi-\xi_k}{\xi_j-\xi_k},
\qquad \ell_j(\xi_i)=\delta_{ij},\qquad
u_h=\sum_j u_j\ell_j.
Here the coefficients u_j are nodal values. In a modal expansion, the coefficients are polynomial amplitudes. For the same polynomial, the change of representation is
u_i=\sum_j V_{ij}a_j,\qquad V_{ij}=P_j(\xi_i),\qquad a=V^{-1}u.
The notebook compares equispaced nodes and Gauss–Lobatto–Legendre (GLL) nodes. It reports the condition number of this Legendre Vandermonde; that number depends on normalization and is not the condition number of a complete PDE solve. Endpoint clustering can help interpolation, but does not remove Gibbs oscillations at a jump.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.text:
With p+1 points, Gauss–Legendre quadrature integrates polynomials through degree 2p+1. GLL includes the endpoints and integrates through degree 2p−1. Its interior points are the zeros of P'_p, and its weights are
w_i=\frac{2}{p(p+1)P_p(\xi_i)^2},\qquad p\geq1.
Products of degree-p basis functions can have degree 2p. Consequently, GLL collocation gives a quadrature mass diag(w), while the exactly integrated GLL nodal mass generally has off-diagonal entries. On an affine interval with unit weight, their difference is rank one. The highest Legendre squared norm is 2/p under GLL quadrature, instead of 2/(2p+1). The notebook lets you switch between both matrices. These facts, and an efficient correction, are derived in Teukolsky's mass-matrix note.
For constant-coefficient stiffness, the polynomial degree is at most 2p−2, so the same GLL rule is sufficient. Nonlinear fluxes and variable metrics can require additional quadrature or a suitable split formulation; a diagonal mass alone is not a nonlinear stability guarantee. DLMF §3.5 explains Gaussian quadrature more generally.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.text:
An unweighted L2 Legendre projection uses integral moments:
a_k=\frac{2k+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}f(\xi)P_k(\xi)\,d\xi.
Nodal interpolation instead matches f at the chosen nodes. They agree for every polynomial of degree at most p, but need not agree for other functions. For exp(ξ), the notebook shows rapidly decreasing errors as p increases. For sign(ξ), the displayed overshoot and slow convergence expose the loss of smoothness; neither approximation supplies a shock limiter. The jump is integrated on two separate half-intervals, and interpolation explicitly uses sign(0)=0. L2 errors are integrated with 80-point Gauss rules on each half.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.section: Quadrilaterals and triangles have different polynomial spaces#
records.text:
On a quadrilateral, a tensor basis takes products of one-dimensional functions:
\phi_{ij}(\xi,\eta)=\ell_i(\xi)\ell_j(\eta),\qquad
0\leq i,j\leq p.
This Q_p space has (p+1)^2 functions. A triangle's total-degree P_p space has (p+1)(p+2)/2. Thus Q2 has nine degrees of freedom, while triangular P2 has six. The cell topology determines which reference map and trace connectivity are needed. DefElement's Lagrange definition distinguishes these spaces and nodal variants.
On the reference triangle (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), barycentric coordinates are λ0=1−ξ−η, λ1=ξ, λ2=η. The P1 vertex functions are λ_i. P2 has vertex functions λ_i(2λ_i−1) and edge functions 4λ_iλ_j. They form a partition of unity and reproduce quadratic fields; they are not an orthogonal basis. The notebook colors each of these six shape functions on the actual triangle.
Orthogonal modal triangle bases can instead be built from suitably weighted Jacobi polynomials in collapsed coordinates, including the Dubiner (1991) construction. A rectangular Legendre tensor product restricted to a triangle does not automatically retain orthogonality. This edition implements P1/P2 nodal triangles and quadrilateral tensor evaluation; a Dubiner implementation remains additional work.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.section: Other orthogonal families and their measures#
records.text:
Orthogonality always includes a domain and a weight. Changing either changes the inner product. The notebook also tabulates Chebyshev T modes and demonstrates their nonorthogonality under unit weight. The remaining families below are mathematical reading connections. Conventions follow DLMF §18.2 and §18.3.
Chebyshev T_n: T_n(cos θ)=cos(nθ), on [-1,1], weight (1−ξ²)^−1/2. Useful for endpoint-clustered spectral interpolation. They are not mutually orthogonal under the unweighted finite-element mass integral.
Jacobi: P_n^(α,β), weight (1−ξ)^α(1+ξ)^β on [-1,1], α,β>−1. This family includes Legendre and, after normalization, Chebyshev; weighted coordinate transforms connect it to simplex bases.
Hermite: physicists' H_n has weight exp(−ξ²) on the real line; probabilists' He_n uses exp(−ξ²/2). These are different conventions. Orthogonal Hermite polynomials are distinct from the endpoint value/derivative Hermite interpolation used by CIP.
Generalized Laguerre: L_n^(α) uses ξ^α exp(−ξ) on [0,∞), α>−1. It addresses a semi-infinite domain rather than an ordinary bounded mesh cell.
Fourier modes: exp(ikx) are orthogonal on a periodic interval with matching integer wave numbers. They form a global periodic basis rather than a mesh-local polynomial family; the spectral advection example uses these modes.

records.title: Orthogonal polynomials and mesh basis functions
records.text:

Tests check continuous Legendre orthogonality, GLL exactness limits, cardinal interpolation, polynomial reproduction, partition of unity, derivative reproduction, the GLL summation-by-parts identity, rank-one mass difference and physical Jacobian scaling. The existing DG solver remains restricted to scalar periodic P0/P1/P2 advection.
The published reference-element source is available from the Legendre method record. Saved arrays and source hashes accompany the figure. This adds reference-element building blocks, not a general curved-mesh assembly or a higher-order fluid solver.

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
For the representation behind DG and spectral examples, see orthogonal polynomials and element bases: Legendre modes, nodal transforms, quadrature, and their mass matrices.
Each 1D Problem stores the equation, domain, final time, boundaries, initial
condition, reference solution, and citation keys. get_problem(name) exposes
the same definition to every method. The last array axis contains variables:
Euler uses (ρ,ρu,E), shallow water uses (h,hu), and isothermal flow uses (ρ,ρu).

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
Linear advection uses periodic [0,1], speed a, and initial data sin(2πx).
The exact translated solution compares finite differences, DG, and Fourier
methods. DG uses modal Legendre P0/P1/P2, upwind boundary fluxes, and SSPRK3.
Distinguish the spatial order of Pp from the third-order time integrator.
DG has elements × (p+1) unknowns. Fourier integrates the linear modes exactly
in time; the gallery does not establish an equal-cost or equal-degree-of-freedom
ranking. Nonlinear products, dealiasing, and Gibbs treatments are future work.
entropy-wave uses Euler data ρ=1+0.2sin(2πx), u=1,p=1,γ=1.4, periodic
[0,1], and t=1. Only density translates, giving an exact reference for smooth
accuracy and periodic conservation. Isothermal Euler has no independent energy
or entropy variable and does not support this same Euler entropy-wave problem.

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
Sod: [0,1], x0=0.5, left (ρ,u,p)=(1,0,1), right (0.125,0,0.1),
γ=1.4, and t=0.2. Boundaries use zero-gradient extrapolation; the main waves
do not reach them before the final time. The exact Riemann solver finds the
matching pressure by bisection and samples shocks, contacts, and rarefaction
fans. Exact solutions containing a vacuum are unsupported.
Sod (1978),
exact-solution implementation reference.
Lax: [-5,5], x0=0, left (0.445,0.698,3.528), right (0.5,0,0.571),
γ=1.4, t=1.3, and extrapolation boundaries. The Lax test and the
Lax–Friedrichs algorithm are different namesakes. These are standard parameters
from later literature; the original 1954 paper's table has not been directly
matched here.
Shu–Osher: [-5,5], x0=-4, t=1.8, γ=1.4, left
(3.857143,2.629369,10.33333), and right (1+0.2sin(5x),0,1).
Ghost states are fixed to the initial conditions evaluated at the domain ends.
There is no exact final-time reference; the first-edition figure compares
MUSCL and WENO numerical results.
Shu–Osher (1989),
adopted parameters in Quokka, §3.1.5.

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
double-rarefaction uses [0,1], x0=0.5, left (1,-2,0.4), right
(1,2,0.4), γ=1.4, and t=0.15. This strong expansion is commonly called
the 1–2–3 problem. The selected positivity test uses piecewise-constant
reconstruction with HLLE. It does not transfer a positivity guarantee to
high-order MUSCL or WENO.
Einfeldt et al. (1991).

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
dam-break solves flat-bottom shallow water with g=1, left h=2, right
h=1, u=0, [0,1], and t=0.1. Dry beds, topographic sources,
well-balanced discretization, and wetting/drying are unsupported.
isothermal uses p=cs²ρ, cs=1, left ρ=1, right ρ=0.125, and u=0
on the same domain and time interval. Both use extrapolation boundaries.
First-edition checks compare solvers, admissible states, and conservative
form. The reference library now supplies semi-analytic
Riemann states and conserved cell means for the equation gallery. The original
Problem.reference callbacks for these two cases remain unset; use
get_reference for the new evaluations.
LeVeque (2002).

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
Rusanov and HLL support Euler, shallow water, and isothermal flow. HLLC, Roe,
and HLLE currently support ideal-gas Euler only. HLL uses minimum/maximum
local acoustic speeds; HLLE uses Einfeldt-type estimates including Roe averages.
Roe applies quadratic entropy smoothing to acoustic eigenvalues with
δ=0.1ã, leaving the contact eigenvalue unchanged. This is neither a
low-density positivity fix nor a general entropy-stable flux construction.
MUSCL uses selectable minmod (default), Superbee, MC, van Leer, or clipped
van Albada reconstruction in primitive variables; see limiters.
WENO5-JS is a
componentwise finite-difference implementation with pointwise fluxes and
global LF splitting. A separate reconstruction chapter below adds characteristics
and WENO-Z; this original solver remains unchanged. Fully discrete positivity
preservation is still future work. A separate advanced limiter
exhibit implements TVB modified minmod and positive Euler reconstruction scaling;
neither is coupled to these Euler time updates. Errors are labeled pointwise: finite-volume cell
averages and finite-difference point values are not strictly interchangeable.
See MHD for Orszag–Tang definitions and limits, and
elliptic problems for diffusion and Poisson cases.

records.title: Benchmark library
records.section: Matching the benchmark to the scheme#
records.text: The original KEEP exhibit uses a smooth isentropic vortex and conservation diagnostics. Its bare central flux has no shock stabilization and is not presented as a Sod/DMR solver. The movie guide separates those smooth computations from shock-capturing and MHD movies, and keeps steady fields as still images.

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text:
The equation gallery adds Burgers and LWR traffic
Riemann problems with exact cell-integrated references, plus advection and heat
mode tests. It also connects the existing Sod, wet dam-break and isothermal
baselines, with each reference convention explicitly labeled.

records.title: Benchmark library
records.text: The new reconstruction chapter and interactive comparison add limited parabolic FV, conservative characteristics, FD WENO-Z and an explicit AUSM-family baseline. The original code described above remains a componentwise baseline. Planar shock sensitivity and Roe's Property U have separate verification.
